Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A$ be invertible. Then the inversion map is real Fr\'echet differentiable
at $A$, and for every direction $H$,

$$D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $p\ge1$, $\mu\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$. Define the component function

$$\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma):=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.$$

The component law is $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, the $p$-dimensional normal law with mean $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$. The separate local normalization result proves that $\phi_p$ is its Lebesgue density.

A finite $K$-component Gaussian mixture has an integer $K\ge1$, weights $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K>0$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1$, means $\mu_k\in\mathbb R^p$, and symmetric positive-definite covariance matrices $\Sigma_k\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$. Its density is

$$f_\theta(x):=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\phi_p(x;\mu_k,\Sigma_k),$$

where $\theta=((\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k))_{k=1}^K$. For a positive integer $n$ and an ordered sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ modeled as conditionally independent observations from this mixture, define the likelihood $L(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\prod_{i=1}^n f_\theta(x_i)$ and log likelihood $\ell(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\sum_{i=1}^n\log f_\theta(x_i)$. The responsibility weight of component $k$ for observation $x_i$ is

$$\gamma_{ik}(\theta):=\frac{\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}.$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

derivations.claim: By [F8], write $\Sigma=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $U^{\mathsf T}U=I$. For a unit eigenvector $u_j$, $\lambda_j=u_j^{\mathsf T}\Sigma u_j>0$. Define $A:=U\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_p})U^{\mathsf T}$. Its eigenvalues are the positive numbers $\sqrt{\lambda_j}$, so it is symmetric positive definite and invertible; in this basis, both $A^2$ and $\Sigma$ have diagonal entries $\lambda_j$, and both $A^{-2}$ and $\Sigma^{-1}$ have diagonal entries $1/\lambda_j$. By determinant multiplicativity and transpose invariance, $(\det U)^2=\det(U^{\mathsf T}U)=\det I=1$. Applying multiplicativity to the displayed diagonalizations and the triangular determinant formula to the diagonal matrices gives $\det\Sigma=(\det U)^2\prod_j\lambda_j=\prod_j\lambda_j$ and $\det A=(\det U)^2\prod_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}=\prod_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}=\sqrt{\det\Sigma}>0$.

By [F2] and [F4], the joint law of $Z$ is the product of its standard-normal marginals. Define $g(y):=\prod_{j=1}^p\phi_1(y_j)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}e^{-\|y\|_2^2/2}$. Tonelli [F5] and the product-measure identity [F6] give $\int_{\mathbb R^p}g\,d\lambda_p=\prod_{j=1}^p\int_{\mathbb R}\phi_1\,d\lambda_1=1$ and, for every Borel rectangle $R=\prod_{j=1}^p B_j$, $\int_R g\,d\lambda_p=\prod_{j=1}^p\int_{B_j}\phi_1\,d\lambda_1$. Thus $g\,d\lambda_p$ and the product law of $Z$ are probability measures agreeing on rectangles. The rational half-open rectangles form a generating pi-system; $(-N,N]^p$ is an increasing exhaustion from it, and the common rectangle values make their measures equal and finite on every such box. Hence [F7] identifies the measures. AC supplies countable choice for the product-Lebesgue identity [F6].

Let $T(y)=\mu+Ay$. By step 1.1, $A$ is invertible, so $T$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^p$ with $|\det DT|=\det A$. The linear measure-scaling result [F10] confirms this is the Lebesgue volume factor. The displayed function $\phi_p$ is continuous and positive, so $f(x)=\mathbf1_E(x)\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)$ is nonnegative Borel for every Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^p$. AC supplies the countable-choice assumption of [F9] by [F12]. Apply [F9] to $f$ and the change of variables by $T$ to obtain $\int_E\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)\,dx=\int_{T^{-1}(E)}\phi_p(T(y);\mu,\Sigma)\det A\,dy.$ For $x=T(y)$, $x-\mu=Ay$ and $A^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}A=A A^{-2}A=I$. Thus the exponent in [F1] becomes $-\|y\|_2^2/2$, while $(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\det A=1$ by step 1.1. Hence $\phi_p(T(y);\mu,\Sigma)\det A=g(y)$. The last integral equals $\int_{T^{-1}(E)}g(y)\,dy=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ by step 1.2 and the definition of $X$. Thus $\phi_p$ is the Lebesgue density of $X$.

By [F3], $X$ has law $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$. Step 2.1 identifies that law on every Borel set with integration against $\phi_p$; taking $E=\mathbb R^p$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R^p}\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)\,dx=\mathbb P(X\in\mathbb R^p)=1$. Nonnegativity follows directly from [F1] and $\det\Sigma>0$ in step 1.1.

Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ be observed vectors, and let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\in\mathbb R^p$ be centers. A labeling is a vector $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\{1,\ldots,K\}^n$, and its $k$th cluster is $C_k(z):=\{i:z_i=k\}$. For $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_p)\in\mathbb R^p$, set $\|v\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^p v_j^2$. The K-means objective is

$$J(z,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K):=\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i-\mu_{z_i}\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k(z)}\|x_i-\mu_k\|_2^2.$$

An empty cluster contributes zero to the sum.

**Input.** Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$, and supply initial centers $\mu_1^{(0)},\ldots,\mu_K^{(0)}\in\mathbb R^p$.

**Initialization.** Assign each $x_i$ to a nearest initial center, choosing the smallest center index in a tie. Denote these labels by $z_i^{(0)}$.

**Iteration.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$:

1. With the current centers fixed, assign each $x_i$ to a nearest center. If its current label $z_i^{(t)}$ is among the nearest-center indices, retain $z_i^{(t)}$; otherwise choose the smallest nearest-center index. Call the resulting labels $z_i^{(t+1)}$.
2. For each nonempty cluster $C_k^{(t+1)}:=\{i:z_i^{(t+1)}=k\}$, set
   $$\mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{1}{|C_k^{(t+1)}|}\sum_{i\in C_k^{(t+1)}}x_i.$$
   If $C_k^{(t+1)}$ is empty, set $\mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\mu_k^{(t)}$.
3. If both $z^{(t+1)}=z^{(t)}$ and $\mu^{(t+1)}=\mu^{(t)}$, return these labels and centers. Otherwise continue with the updated labels and centers.

The procedure makes no global-minimization claim. Its termination under these tie rules is proved separately.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

derivations.claim: Fix the current centers. For each observation, the old label is one of the available centers, so choosing a nearest center cannot increase its squared distance. If the label changes, its new distance is strictly smaller: an equal-distance tie would retain the old label by [F2]. Summing the pointwise inequalities gives nonincrease of $J$, strict when any label changes.

Fix a nonempty cluster $C$ and set $T(u)=(u)_{i\in C}$ from $\mathbb R^p$ to $(\mathbb R^p)^C$, with product inner product, and $b=(x_i)_{i\in C}$. For $u,v\in\mathbb R^p$, $\langle Tu,Tv\rangle=|C|\langle u,v\rangle$, so $T^*T=|C|I$; also $\langle Tu,b\rangle=\langle u,\sum_{i\in C}x_i\rangle$, so $T^*b=\sum_{i\in C}x_i$. Minimizing $\|Tu-b\|$ is equivalent to minimizing its square, since squaring is increasing on nonnegative reals. Thus [F3] gives the unique minimizer $\bar x_C=|C|^{-1}\sum_{i\in C}x_i$; uniqueness follows because $T$ is injective for nonempty $C$. Replacing a center by this mean cannot increase the cluster contribution and strictly decreases it if the old center differed. Empty clusters contribute zero and retain their centers.

A nonterminal iteration changes either the labels or at least one nonempty center. By steps 1.1 and 1.2, its full assignment-and-center update therefore strictly decreases $J$. After every center update, the nonempty centers are the means for that labeling, so the resulting objective value is determined by the labeling alone; empty centers do not affect it. A labeling cannot recur after a nonterminal update, because its objective value would then repeat despite strict decrease. There are only $K^n$ labelings, so only finitely many nonterminal iterations are possible and the algorithm terminates.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma):=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.$$

The component law is $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, the $p$-dimensional normal law with mean $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$. The separate local normalization result proves that $\phi_p$ is its Lebesgue density.

A finite $K$-component Gaussian mixture has an integer $K\ge1$, weights $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K>0$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1$, means $\mu_k\in\mathbb R^p$, and symmetric positive-definite covariance matrices $\Sigma_k\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$. Its density is

$$f_\theta(x):=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\phi_p(x;\mu_k,\Sigma_k),$$

where $\theta=((\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k))_{k=1}^K$. For a positive integer $n$ and an ordered sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ modeled as conditionally independent observations from this mixture, define the likelihood $L(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\prod_{i=1}^n f_\theta(x_i)$ and log likelihood $\ell(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\sum_{i=1}^n\log f_\theta(x_i)$. $$\gamma_{ik}(\theta):=\frac{\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}.$$

[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for

monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm

measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since

[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$

[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts

[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by

$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Let $p\ge1$ and let $A_0,A_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices. For $0<t<1$ and $A_0\ne A_1$,

$$\log\det((1-t)A_0+tA_1)>(1-t)\log\det A_0+t\log\det A_1.$$

If $A_0=A_1$, equality holds. Thus $A\mapsto\log\det A$ is strictly concave on the positive-definite cone.

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Since $S_k$ is visibly symmetric, it is positive definite.

A **jointly measurable latent-variable density** is a specified function
$$p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\longrightarrow[0,\infty]$$

$$\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\, (\nu\otimes\mu)(d(x,z))=1\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$

observed marginal density is
$$m(\theta,x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz).$$

$$q(z\mid\theta,x):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m(\theta,x)}.$$

At each valid iterate $\theta_t$, set $q_t:=q_{\theta_t}^x$ and define
$$Q(\theta\mid\theta_t):=\int_{\mathsf Z}\log p(\theta,x,z)\,q_t(z)\,\mu(dz)$$
only for candidates where this integral is finite. Use $\log0=-\infty$ and set $q_t|\log p|=0$ wherever $q_t=0$. The Q integral itself is choice-free. To test finite KL when $q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu$, assume AC as required by [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; when absolute continuity fails, $D=+\infty$ by that definition without AC. An **admissible candidate** $\theta$ also satisfies $0<m_\theta(x)<\infty$, $q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu$, and
$$D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu)<\infty,$$
where the direction of $D$ is that of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Require $\int q_t|\log p(\theta,x,\cdot)|\,d\mu<\infty$ for each candidate and $\int q_t|\log p(\theta_t,x,\cdot)|\,d\mu<\infty$ for the current iterate.

**Output.** Emit the iterate sequence beginning with $\theta_0$. If a stopping condition occurs after $T$ successful updates, return the finite list $(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_T)$ and a status recording the first unavailable condition or selector result; do not append a failed candidate. If no stopping condition occurs, the emitted sequence is infinite and there is no finite stopping status.

**Procedure.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$, check that $0<m_{\theta_t}(x)<\infty$; if not, return the current list with status `stopped: invalid current marginal`. Form $q_t$ and $Q(\cdot\mid\theta_t)$ on admissible candidates. If $Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ is not finite, return with status `stopped: current Q is not finite`. Call the supplied selector. In **exact mode**, its candidate set must consist of admissible candidates and contain $\theta_t$; it returns an attained maximizer of $Q$ on that set, or `unavailable` if no attained maximum is available. In **generalized mode**, it returns any admissible $\theta_{t+1}$ with $Q(\theta_{t+1}\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$, or `unavailable` if no such update is supplied. If the selector returns `unavailable`, return with status `stopped: no required update supplied`; otherwise append its candidate and continue. The procedure asserts no convergence or global-optimality property and makes no assertion for a candidate that loses current latent support.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $p(\theta,x,z)$ be a jointly measurable normalized complete-data density as in [[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]], and fix observed data $x$. Put $m_\theta(x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$. Let $\theta_t$ and $\theta$ satisfy $0<m_{\theta_t}(x),m_\theta(x)<\infty$. Define $q_t(z)=p(\theta_t,x,z)/m_{\theta_t}(x)$ and $q_\theta^x(z)=p(\theta,x,z)/m_\theta(x)$. Assume
$$q_t\mu\ll q_\theta^x\mu,\qquad \int q_t(z)\bigl(|\log p(\theta_t,x,z)|+|\log p(\theta,x,z)|\bigr)\,\mu(dz)<\infty,$$
and $D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu)<\infty$. Use $\log0=-\infty$ and set $q_t|\log p|=0$ wherever $q_t=0$. Then, with $Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)=\int q_t(z)\log p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$,
$$\ell_x(\theta)-\ell_x(\theta_t) =Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)-Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t) +D(q_t\mu\|q_\theta^x\mu).$$
Consequently, any admissible update with $Q(\theta\mid\theta_t)\ge Q(\theta_t\mid\theta_t)$ does not decrease $\ell_x$. An exact M-step has this property when its maximum is attained over an admissible candidate set containing $\theta_t$. No equality-of-parameter conclusion is asserted when the KL divergence is zero.

Assume AC. Let $n,p,K$ be positive integers, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ have affine span $\mathbb R^p$ (equivalently, no nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ makes $v^{\mathsf T}x_i$ constant over all $i$), and let $\theta=((\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k))_{k=1}^K$ be a finite Gaussian-mixture parameter with every $\pi_k>0$ and every $\Sigma_k$ symmetric positive definite. Define

$$\gamma_{ik}=\frac{\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)},\qquad N_k=\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik},\qquad \bar x_k=\frac1{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}x_i,$$

and

$$S_k=\frac1{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\bar x_k)(x_i-\bar x_k)^{\mathsf T}.$$

For a candidate parameter $\vartheta=((\rho_k,m_k,V_k))_{k=1}^K$ in the same domain, let

$$Q(\vartheta\mid\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K\gamma_{ik}\log\!\left(\rho_k\phi_p(x_i;m_k,V_k)\right).$$

Then every $N_k$ is positive, $\sum_kN_k=n$, every $S_k$ is positive definite, and the unique global maximizer of $Q(\vartheta\mid\theta)$ over all positive mixture weights summing to one, means in $\mathbb R^p$, and symmetric positive-definite covariances is

$$\rho_k^*=N_k/n,\qquad m_k^*=\bar x_k,\qquad V_k^*=S_k.$$

In particular, the displayed E-step responsibilities and M-step update formulas are well-defined and attain this maximum.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

Let $A$ be invertible. Then the inversion map is real Fr\'echet differentiable
at $A$, and for every direction $H$,

$$D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}.$$

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

derivations.claim: Let $\Theta_K$ be the set of mixture parameters in [F1], let $Y=(\mathbb R^p)^n$ with product Lebesgue measure $\nu=\lambda_p^{\otimes n}$, and let $Z=\{1,\ldots,K\}^n$ with counting measure $\#(B):=|B|$ for $B\subseteq Z$. The parameter domain is Borel: the positive-weight simplex is relatively open in its affine hyperplane, and the SPD cone is open as follows. For a symmetric positive-definite matrix $A$, the spectral theorem [F15] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. Every eigenvalue $\lambda$ has a unit eigenvector $u$ with $\lambda=u^{\mathsf T}Au>0$, so the least eigenvalue $\lambda_{\min}(A)$ is positive. For a symmetric perturbation $E$, define $\|E\|_F:=(\sum_{i,j}e_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. Applying [F19] to the finite lists $(e_{ij})$ and $(v_iv_j)$ gives $|v^{\mathsf T}Ev|\le\|E\|_F(\sum_{i,j}v_i^2v_j^2)^{1/2}=\|E\|_F\|v\|_2^2$. Therefore, whenever $\|E\|_F<\lambda_{\min}(A)$, $$v^{\mathsf T}(A+E)v\ge(\lambda_{\min}(A)-\|E\|_F)\|v\|_2^2>0$$ for every nonzero $v$, so $A+E$ is positive definite. This supplies a relative open neighborhood of each $A$ in the symmetric-matrix subspace. For each fixed $z\in Z$, the formula below is continuous in $(\eta,y)\in\Theta_K\times Y$: determinants and inverses are continuous on the SPD cone by [F15], and the remaining operations are sums, products, and exponentials. A continuous map on this Borel subspace has Borel preimages relative to it; those relative Borel sets are ambient Borel. The product-Borel identification for Euclidean factors [F16] and finite discreteness of $Z$ then make the function jointly measurable for the required product sigma-algebra.

Define the complete-data density, relative to $
u$ times counting measure on $Z$, by $p(\eta,y,z):=\prod_{i=1}^n\pi_{z_i}\phi_p(y_i;\mu_{z_i},\Sigma_{z_i}).$ Repeated use of [F9] constructs the finite product measures, including $
u\otimes\#$, and preserves sigma-finiteness. AC supplies the countable-choice premise of [F11] by [F10]; repeated use of [F11] then identifies $
u=\lambda_p^{\otimes n}$ with Euclidean Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^{pn}$. For each component, [F1,F2] and finite-sum additivity [F18] give $\int f_\eta(y_i)\,\lambda_p(dy_i)=\sum_k\pi_k=1$. Distributing the finite sum over labels gives $\sum_{z\in Z}p(\eta,y,z)=\prod_i f_\eta(y_i)$. Repeated Tonelli integration [F12] therefore gives $\sum_{z\in Z}\int_Yp(\eta,y,z)\,
u(dy)=\int_Y\prod_i f_\eta(y_i)\,
u(dy)=\prod_i\int_{\mathbb R^p}f_\eta(y_i)\,\lambda_p(dy_i)=1.$ Thus $p$ is normalized on each parameter fibre as required by [F3].

For a fixed observed sample $x_{1:n}$, summing the complete density over the finite label set yields $m_\eta(x_{1:n})=\sum_{z\in Z}p(\eta,x_{1:n},z)=\prod_i\sum_k\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)=\prod_i f_\eta(x_i).$ Every factor is finite and strictly positive by [F1,F2], so this marginal is positive and finite. Its logarithm is exactly the likelihood $\ell(\eta;x_{1:n})$ in the statement. By [F4], every normalized posterior $q_\eta^{x_{1:n}}(z)=p(\eta,x_{1:n},z)/m_\eta(x_{1:n})$ is a probability mass function. More explicitly it is $q_\eta^{x_{1:n}}(z)=\prod_i\gamma_{i,z_i}(\eta),$ and every one of its finitely many masses is positive.

At any current parameter $\theta$ and its exact update $\theta'$, both posterior measures obtained from the probability masses in step 3.1 by [F17] are strictly positive on the same finite label set. Hence $q_\theta^{x_{1:n}}\ll q_{\theta'}^{x_{1:n}}$, and the directional KL divergence is a sum of finitely many finite terms by [F8], so it is finite. For each $z$, $p(\theta,x_{1:n},z)$ and $p(\theta',x_{1:n},z)$ are strictly positive and finite; their logarithms are finite. The posterior expectations of the absolute log densities are finite sums and therefore finite. Thus every admissibility condition in [F5,F6] holds for this current/candidate pair.

The posterior in step 3.1 factors over observations. Taking the finite expectation of the complete log density gives $\sum_{z\in Z}q_\theta^{x_{1:n}}(z)\log p(\vartheta,x_{1:n},z)=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^K\gamma_{ik}(\theta)\log\!\left(\rho_k\phi_p(x_i;m_k,V_k)\right)=Q(\vartheta\mid\theta),$ where $Q$ is the function in [F7]. Indeed, expand $\log p$ as the sum over $i$, sum first over $z_i=k$, and use $\sum_{j\ne i}\sum_{z_j}\gamma_{j,z_j}(\theta)=1$ for each other coordinate. This is a finite-sum identity, and all terms are finite by step 3.1.

The local exact M-step result [F7] says $\theta'$ globally maximizes this same Q over the full mixture domain. Step 4.1 verifies that both $\theta$ and $\theta'$ are admissible, so the two-point candidate set $\{\theta,\theta'\}$ is admissible and contains the current parameter; the global maximizer $\theta'$ is therefore an attained maximizer over this set as required by the exact mode of [F5]. Consequently $Q(\theta'\mid\theta)\ge Q(\theta\mid\theta)$. Applying the identity and nonnegativity conclusion of [F6], with the verified conditions from step 4.1, yields $\ell(\theta';x_{1:n})-\ell(\theta;x_{1:n})=Q(\theta'\mid\theta)-Q(\theta\mid\theta)+D(q_\theta^{x_{1:n}}\|q_{\theta'}^{x_{1:n}})\ge0.$ Thus one exact update does not decrease observed log likelihood.

Initially $\theta_0$ is in the mixture domain by hypothesis. If $\theta_t$ is in that domain, step 3.1 supplies positive finite marginals and positive responsibilities, and [F7] supplies the next positive weights and SPD covariances; hence $\theta_{t+1}$ is again in the domain. Induction gives valid parameters through $T$, and step 5.1 applies at each $t<T$, proving every displayed likelihood inequality. This proves the claim without asserting strict increase or convergence.

Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$ be observed vectors, and let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\in\mathbb R^p$ be centers. A labeling is a vector $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\{1,\ldots,K\}^n$, and its $k$th cluster is $C_k(z):=\{i:z_i=k\}$. For $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_p)\in\mathbb R^p$, set $\|v\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^p v_j^2$. The K-means objective is

$$J(z,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K):=\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i-\mu_{z_i}\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k(z)}\|x_i-\mu_k\|_2^2.$$

An empty cluster contributes zero to the sum.

**Input.** Let $n,p$ be positive integers, let $1\le K\le n$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^p$, and supply initial centers $\mu_1^{(0)},\ldots,\mu_K^{(0)}\in\mathbb R^p$.

**Initialization.** Assign each $x_i$ to a nearest initial center, choosing the smallest center index in a tie. Denote these labels by $z_i^{(0)}$.

**Iteration.** For $t=0,1,2,\ldots$:

1. With the current centers fixed, assign each $x_i$ to a nearest center. If its current label $z_i^{(t)}$ is among the nearest-center indices, retain $z_i^{(t)}$; otherwise choose the smallest nearest-center index. Call the resulting labels $z_i^{(t+1)}$.
2. For each nonempty cluster $C_k^{(t+1)}:=\{i:z_i^{(t+1)}=k\}$, set
   $$\mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\frac{1}{|C_k^{(t+1)}|}\sum_{i\in C_k^{(t+1)}}x_i.$$
   If $C_k^{(t+1)}$ is empty, set $\mu_k^{(t+1)}:=\mu_k^{(t)}$.
3. If both $z^{(t+1)}=z^{(t)}$ and $\mu^{(t+1)}=\mu^{(t)}$, return these labels and centers. Otherwise continue with the updated labels and centers.

The procedure makes no global-minimization claim. Its termination under these tie rules is proved separately.

derivations.claim: From initial centers $(0,11/10)$, the nearest labels are $(1,2,2,2)$: the respective comparisons are $0<121/100$, $1>1/100$, $4>81/100$, and $9>361/100$. The mean update gives centers $0$ and $(1+2+3)/3=2$.

From initial centers $(3,19/10)$, nearest labels are $(2,2,2,1)$: observations $0,1,2$ are strictly nearer $19/10$, while $3$ equals the first center. Their means become $3$ for cluster $1$ and $(0+1+2)/3=1$ for cluster $2$.

From initial centers $(1/2,5/2)$, nearest labels are $(1,1,2,2)$. The means of these clusters are again $1/2$ and $5/2$, so labels and centers are unchanged and the procedure stops. The objective is $4(1/2)^2=1$.

With centers $(0,2)$, observations $0,2,3$ keep labels $1,2,2$ by strict nearest comparisons; observation $1$ is at distance $1$ from each center and retains its current label $2$. The labels remain $(1,2,2,2)$, so their means remain $(0,2)$ and the procedure stops. The objective is $(0-0)^2+(1-2)^2+(2-2)^2+(3-2)^2=2$.

With centers $(3,1)$, observations $0,1,3$ keep labels $2,2,1$ by strict nearest comparisons; observation $2$ is tied at distance $1$ and retains label $2$. The labels stay $(2,2,2,1)$, their means remain $(3,1)$, and the procedure stops. The objective is $(0-1)^2+(1-1)^2+(2-1)^2+(3-3)^2=2$.

The three explicitly computed terminal states have objective values $2,2,1$, respectively, so they are distinct fixed points and the third has strictly lower objective than the first two. In the first and second runs, changing the tied boundary point to the other cluster would change the fixed partition; under the stated rule it remains with its current label.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $p\ge1$, $\mu\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$. Define the component function

$$\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma):=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.$$

The component law is $N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, the $p$-dimensional normal law with mean $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$. The separate local normalization result proves that $\phi_p$ is its Lebesgue density.

A finite $K$-component Gaussian mixture has an integer $K\ge1$, weights $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K>0$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1$, means $\mu_k\in\mathbb R^p$, and symmetric positive-definite covariance matrices $\Sigma_k\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$. Its density is

$$f_\theta(x):=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\phi_p(x;\mu_k,\Sigma_k),$$

where $\theta=((\pi_k,\mu_k,\Sigma_k))_{k=1}^K$. For a positive integer $n$ and an ordered sample $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ modeled as conditionally independent observations from this mixture, define the likelihood $L(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\prod_{i=1}^n f_\theta(x_i)$ and log likelihood $\ell(\theta;x_{1:n}):=\sum_{i=1}^n\log f_\theta(x_i)$. The responsibility weight of component $k$ for observation $x_i$ is

$$\gamma_{ik}(\theta):=\frac{\pi_k\phi_p(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\phi_p(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}.$$

Assume AC. Let $p\ge1$, let $\mu\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric positive definite. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_p$ be independent standard normal random variables, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_p)^{\mathsf T}$, and set $X=\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$, where $\Sigma^{1/2}$ is the symmetric positive-definite square root. Then the law of $X$ has Lebesgue density

$$\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.$$

In particular, $\phi_p$ is nonnegative and $\int_{\mathbb R^p}\phi_p(x;\mu,\Sigma)\,dx=1$.

Let $n,p,K$ be positive integers, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K\in\mathbb R^p$, and fix positive weights $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K$ with $\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1$. Put $d_{ik}:=\|x_i-\mu_k\|_2^2$, $d_i^*:=\min_{1\le k\le K}d_{ik}$, and $M_i:=\{k:d_{ik}=d_i^*\}$. For every $\sigma>0$, define the normalized soft-assignment weights

$$\rho_{ik}^{(\sigma)}:=\frac{\pi_k\exp(-d_{ik}/(2\sigma^2))}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_j\exp(-d_{ij}/(2\sigma^2))}$$

and the finite-data objective

$$\Psi_\sigma:=-2\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k\exp(-d_{ik}/(2\sigma^2))\right).$$

As $\sigma\downarrow0$, for each $i$ and $k$,

$$\rho_{ik}^{(\sigma)}\longrightarrow\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\pi_k}{\sum_{j\in M_i}\pi_j},&k\in M_i,\\[6pt]0,&k\notin M_i,\end{cases}$$

and

$$\Psi_\sigma\longrightarrow\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^*=\min_{z\in\{1,\ldots,K\}^n}\sum_{i=1}^n d_{i,z_i}.$$

Thus a unique nearest center receives limiting weight one, while tied nearest centers divide limiting weight in proportion to their fixed mixture weights. This is a fixed-parameter finite-data limit and asserts no convergence of EM iterates.

derivations.claim: Substitution in [F1] gives $\phi_1(0;-1,\sigma^2)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}e^{-1/(2\sigma^2)}=\phi_1(0;1,\sigma^2)=:c_\sigma.$ By [F2], $c_\sigma$ is finite and positive under [A1].

The responsibility denominator is $c_\sigma(1/3+2/3)=c_\sigma$. Dividing the two weighted component values by that denominator gives $\gamma_1=(1/3)c_\sigma/c_\sigma=1/3$ and $\gamma_2=(2/3)c_\sigma/c_\sigma=2/3$ for every $\sigma>0$.

Since the vector is constant for all positive $\sigma$, its limit as $\sigma\downarrow0$ is $(1/3,2/3)$, which is not one-hot. Both centers are nearest to $0$, so [F3] gives the same tied-center limit, proportional to the fixed weights.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$

derivations.claim: Let $f_\varepsilon$ be the mixture density. From [F1], $f_\varepsilon(0)=\tfrac12\phi_1(0;0,\varepsilon^2)+\tfrac12\phi_1(0;0,1)\ge\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}\,\varepsilon}.$ Also $f_\varepsilon(1)=\tfrac12\phi_1(1;0,\varepsilon^2)+\tfrac12\phi_1(1;0,1)\ge\frac{e^{-1/2}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}>0.$ These bounds hold for every $\varepsilon>0$, for which both variances are positive; [F2] supplies the stated density interpretation under [A1].

The sample likelihood $L_\varepsilon=f_\varepsilon(0)f_\varepsilon(1)$ therefore satisfies $L_\varepsilon\ge\frac{e^{-1/2}}{8\pi\varepsilon}.$ Given any real $R$, choose $0<\varepsilon<e^{-1/2}/(8\pi e^R)$; then step 1.1 gives $L_\varepsilon>e^R$. By [F3], $\log L_\varepsilon>\log(e^R)=R$. Thus both the likelihood and its log are unbounded above.
